claim: Heart failure is a major public health problem.
source: Heart failure is a major public health problem, and abnormal iron metabolism is common in patients with heart failure.
evidence: This is a general statement about the significance of heart failure as a public health issue, supported by citation to Ponikowski et al., 2016 in the Introduction.

claim: Abnormal iron metabolism is common in patients with heart failure.
source: Heart failure is a major public health problem, and abnormal iron metabolism is common in patients with heart failure.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lavoie, 2020 in the Introduction section.

claim: Iron is necessary for metabolic homeostasis.
source: Although iron is necessary for metabolic homeostasis, it induces a programmed necrosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andrews and Schmidt, 2007 in the Introduction.

claim: Iron induces a programmed necrosis.
source: Although iron is necessary for metabolic homeostasis, it induces a programmed necrosis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dixon et al., 2012 and related work on ferroptosis in the Introduction.

claim: Iron release from ferritin storage is through nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4)-mediated autophagic degradation, known as ferritinophagy.
source: Iron release from ferritin storage is through nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4)-mediated autophagic degradation, known as ferritinophagy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dowdle et al., 2014 and Mancias et al., 2014 in the Introduction.

claim: Deletion of Ncoa4 in mouse hearts reduced left ventricular chamber size 4 weeks after pressure overload.
source: Deletion of Ncoa4 in mouse hearts reduced left ventricular chamber size and improved cardiac function along with the attenuation of the upregulation of ferritinophagy-mediated ferritin degradation 4 weeks after pressure overload.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B showing echocardiographic measurements.

claim: Deletion of Ncoa4 in mouse hearts improved cardiac function 4 weeks after pressure overload.
source: Deletion of Ncoa4 in mouse hearts reduced left ventricular chamber size and improved cardiac function along with the attenuation of the upregulation of ferritinophagy-mediated ferritin degradation 4 weeks after pressure overload.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B showing fractional shortening measurements.

claim: Deletion of Ncoa4 attenuated the upregulation of ferritinophagy-mediated ferritin degradation 4 weeks after pressure overload.
source: Deletion of Ncoa4 in mouse hearts reduced left ventricular chamber size and improved cardiac function along with the attenuation of the upregulation of ferritinophagy-mediated ferritin degradation 4 weeks after pressure overload.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3 showing FTH1 protein levels and colocalization studies.

claim: Free ferrous iron overload was suppressed in NCOA4-deficient hearts after pressure overload.
source: Free ferrous iron overload and increased lipid peroxidation were suppressed in NCOA4-deficient hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A showing iron measurements.

claim: Increased lipid peroxidation was suppressed in NCOA4-deficient hearts after pressure overload.
source: Free ferrous iron overload and increased lipid peroxidation were suppressed in NCOA4-deficient hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A showing MDA and 4-HNE measurements.

claim: Ferrostatin-1 significantly mitigated the development of pressure overload-induced dilated cardiomyopathy in wild-type mice.
source: A potent inhibitor of lipid peroxidation, ferrostatin-1, significantly mitigated the development of pressure overload-induced dilated cardiomyopathy in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 showing echocardiographic and histological measurements.

claim: The activation of ferritinophagy results in the development of heart failure.
source: Thus, the activation of ferritinophagy results in the development of heart failure, whereas inhibition of this process protects the heart against hemodynamic stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that NCOA4 deletion protects against heart failure.

claim: Inhibition of ferritinophagy protects the heart against hemodynamic stress.
source: Thus, the activation of ferritinophagy results in the development of heart failure, whereas inhibition of this process protects the heart against hemodynamic stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that NCOA4 deletion and ferrostatin-1 treatment protect against pressure overload-induced heart failure.

claim: Heart failure is the leading cause of death in developed countries.
source: Heart failure is the leading cause of death in developed countries (Ponikowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ponikowski et al., 2016.

claim: There is substantial evidence to suggest the involvement of oxidative stress and cardiomyocyte death in the pathogenesis of heart failure.
source: There is substantial evidence to suggest the involvement of oxidative stress and cardiomyocyte death in the pathogenesis of heart failure (Whelan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whelan et al., 2010.

claim: Iron metabolism in heart failure patients is dysregulated.
source: Iron metabolism in heart failure patients is dysregulated (Lavoie, 2020), but it remains unclear whether these changes are pathogenetic and detrimental or adaptative and protective for the heart.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lavoie, 2020.

claim: It remains unclear whether iron metabolism changes in heart failure are pathogenetic and detrimental or adaptative and protective for the heart.
source: Iron metabolism in heart failure patients is dysregulated (Lavoie, 2020), but it remains unclear whether these changes are pathogenetic and detrimental or adaptative and protective for the heart.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty in the field, supported by the need for the current study.

claim: Iron is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, metabolite synthesis, and oxygen transport.
source: While iron is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, metabolite synthesis, and oxygen transport (Andrews and Schmidt, 2007), it can generate toxic reactive hydroxyl radicals through the Fenton reaction (Papanikolaou and Pantopoulos, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andrews and Schmidt, 2007.

claim: Iron can generate toxic reactive hydroxyl radicals through the Fenton reaction.
source: While iron is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, metabolite synthesis, and oxygen transport (Andrews and Schmidt, 2007), it can generate toxic reactive hydroxyl radicals through the Fenton reaction (Papanikolaou and Pantopoulos, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papanikolaou and Pantopoulos, 2005.

claim: Iron-dependent necrotic cell death is characterized by iron overload and an increased level of lipid reactive oxygen species.
source: Iron-dependent necrotic cell death is characterized by iron overload and an increased level of lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as lipid hydroperoxides, leading to phospholipid damage, plasma membrane disruption, and caspase- and necrosome-independent cell death (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: Ferroptosis is a form of iron-dependent necrosis.
source: Ferroptosis is a form of iron-dependent necrosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Dixon et al., 2012 and related work.

claim: Multiple molecular components contribute to the execution of ferroptosis, such as transferrin–iron, cystine–glutathione, and glutamine pathways.
source: Multiple molecular components contribute to the execution of ferroptosis, such as transferrin–iron, cystine–glutathione, and glutamine pathways (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2015.

claim: Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) is a phospholipid hydroperoxide-reducing enzyme that uses glutathione as a substrate.
source: Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) is a phospholipid hydroperoxide-reducing enzyme that uses glutathione as a substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPX4 function, supported by citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: The failure of GPX4 to clear lipid ROS leads to lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis.
source: The failure of GPX4 to clear lipid ROS leads to lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Glutamate through the glutamine-fueled intracellular metabolic process glutaminolysis induces ferroptosis.
source: Glutamate through the glutamine-fueled intracellular metabolic process glutaminolysis induces ferroptosis (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2015.

claim: Ferroptosis has been implicated in the pathological process associated with ROS-induced tissue injury, such as ischemia/reperfusion in the brain, kidney, and heart.
source: Ferroptosis has been implicated in the pathological process associated with ROS-induced tissue injury, such as ischemia/reperfusion in the brain, kidney, and heart (Fang et al., 2019; Linkermann et al., 2014; Tuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fang et al., 2019; Linkermann et al., 2014; Tuo et al., 2017.

claim: Iron is stored in ferritin protein complexes in the cell to prevent an increase in the size of the labile iron pool that normally follows iron overload.
source: Iron is stored in ferritin protein complexes in the cell to prevent an increase in the size of the labile iron pool that normally follows iron overload.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ferritin function, supported by citation to Arosio et al., 2009.

claim: Ferritin is a ubiquitously expressed cytosolic heteropolymer composed of H-chains (FTH1) and L-chains (FTL).
source: Ferritin is a ubiquitously expressed cytosolic heteropolymer composed of H-chains (FTH1) and L-chains (FTL) (Arosio et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arosio et al., 2009.

claim: FTH1 has ferroxidase activity and sequestrates ferrous iron (Fe2+) from the Fenton reaction.
source: FTH1 has ferroxidase activity and sequestrates ferrous iron (Fe2 ) from the Fenton reaction in which the spontaneous oxidation to ferric iron (Fe3 ) donates single electrons to transform innocuous hydrogen peroxide to highly toxic hydroxyl free radicals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FTH1 function, supported by citation to Arosio et al., 2009.

claim: In the case of iron overload, ferritin subunits are induced by inactivating the iron regulatory protein (IREB)/iron-responsive element pathway.
source: In the case of iron overload, ferritin subunits are induced by inactivating the iron regulatory protein (IREB)/iron-responsive element pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about iron regulation, supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2012.

claim: Under conditions of iron deficiency or increased iron requirement, ferritin is degraded and mediated through a selective form of autophagy, called ferritinophagy.
source: By contrast, under conditions of iron deficiency or increased iron requirement, ferritin is degraded and mediated through a selective form of autophagy, called ferritinophagy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dowdle et al., 2014 and Mancias et al., 2014.

claim: Nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4) is a cargo receptor for ferritinophagy that interacts with FTH1 and promotes the transport of ferritin to the autophagosome for degradation.
source: Nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4) is a cargo receptor for ferritinophagy that interacts with FTH1 and promotes the transport of ferritin to the autophagosome for degradation (Dowdle et al., 2014; Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dowdle et al., 2014 and Mancias et al., 2014.

claim: NCOA4-dependent iron release from ferritin storage is necessary for erythropoiesis.
source: NCOA4-dependent iron release from ferritin storage is necessary for erythropoiesis (Bellelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellelli et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiomyocyte-specific NCOA4-deficient mice were generated.
source: To examine the in vivo role of NCOA4-dependent ferritin degradation in the heart, cardiomyocyte-specific NCOA4-deficient mice were generated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The homozygous floxed Ncoa4 mice (Ncoa4flox/flox) appeared normal and were externally indistinguishable from littermates of other genotypes.
source: The homozygous floxed Ncoa4 mice (Ncoa4flox/flox) appeared normal and were externally indistinguishable from littermates of other genotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental generation of the mice.

claim: The Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio.
source: The Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio (54 and 51 mice, respectively), and they grew to adulthood and were fertile.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on mouse breeding.

claim: The Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice grew to adulthood and were fertile.
source: The Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio (54 and 51 mice, respectively), and they grew to adulthood and were fertile.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental generation of the mice.

claim: The protein levels of NCOA4 were significantly decreased in Ncoa4–/– hearts by 84% compared to control.
source: The protein and mRNA levels of NCOA4 were significantly decreased in Ncoa4–/– hearts by 84% and 81% compared to control, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mRNA levels of NCOA4 were significantly decreased in Ncoa4–/– hearts by 81% compared to control.
source: The protein and mRNA levels of NCOA4 were significantly decreased in Ncoa4–/– hearts by 84% and 81% compared to control, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No differences in any physiological or echocardiographic parameters were observed between the Ncoa4–/– and Ncoa4+/+ mice at baseline.
source: No differences in any physiological or echocardiographic parameters were observed between the Ncoa4–/– and Ncoa4+/+ mice (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: Pressure overload increased the left ventricular (LV) chamber size in Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to sham-operated controls.
source: Pressure overload increased the left ventricular (LV) chamber size, indicated by the end-diastolic and end-systolic LV internal dimensions, and reduced fractional shortening (an index of contractility) in Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to sham-operated controls (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Pressure overload reduced fractional shortening in Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to sham-operated controls.
source: Pressure overload increased the left ventricular (LV) chamber size, indicated by the end-diastolic and end-systolic LV internal dimensions, and reduced fractional shortening (an index of contractility) in Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to sham-operated controls (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pressure overload-induced changes in heart size and function were suppressed in Ncoa4–/– mice.
source: These pressure overload-induced changes in heart size and function were suppressed in Ncoa4–/– mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The calculated LV mass was elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but was significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls.
source: The calculated LV mass, LV weight-to-tibia length ratio, and the cross-sectional area of cardiomyocytes, which are parameters for cardiac hypertrophy, were elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but those were significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The LV weight-to-tibia length ratio was elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but was significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls.
source: The calculated LV mass, LV weight-to-tibia length ratio, and the cross-sectional area of cardiomyocytes, which are parameters for cardiac hypertrophy, were elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but those were significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The cross-sectional area of cardiomyocytes was elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but was significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls.
source: The calculated LV mass, LV weight-to-tibia length ratio, and the cross-sectional area of cardiomyocytes, which are parameters for cardiac hypertrophy, were elevated by pressure overload in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, but those were significantly lower in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice than in TAC-operated controls (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice displayed higher mRNA expression levels of the cardiac remodeling markers, Nppa, Nppb, and Myh7 than TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice.
source: TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice displayed higher mRNA expression levels of the cardiac remodeling markers, Nppa, Nppb, and Myh7 than TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lung weight-to-tibia length ratio was significantly elevated in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to both sham-operated Ncoa4+/+ and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice.
source: Furthermore, the lung weight-to-tibia length ratio, an index of lung congestion, was significantly elevated in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice compared to both sham-operated Ncoa4+/+ and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The extent of pressure overload-induced fibrosis in heart sections in Ncoa4–/– mice was lower than in Ncoa4+/+ mice.
source: The extent of pressure overload-induced fibrosis in heart sections and the mRNA levels of Col1a2 and Col3a1, markers for fibrosis, in Ncoa4–/– mice were lower than in Ncoa4+/+ mice (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mRNA levels of Col1a2 and Col3a1 in Ncoa4–/– mice were lower than in Ncoa4+/+ mice after pressure overload.
source: The extent of pressure overload-induced fibrosis in heart sections and the mRNA levels of Col1a2 and Col3a1, markers for fibrosis, in Ncoa4–/– mice were lower than in Ncoa4+/+ mice (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no differences in echocardiographic parameters between TAC-operated Myh6-Cre+ and Myh6-Cre– mice 4 weeks after TAC.
source: There were no differences in echocardiographic parameters between TAC-operated Myh6-Cre+ and Myh6-Cre– mice 4 weeks after TAC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The overexpression of Cre recombinase in the heart has no effect on pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling.
source: Thus, the overexpression of Cre recombinase in the heart has no effect on pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling.
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NCOA4 deficiency attenuated pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling, including cardiac hypertrophy and dysfunction, chamber dilation, and fibrosis.
source: Taken together, NCOA4 deficiency attenuated pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling, including cardiac hypertrophy and dysfunction, chamber dilation, and fibrosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The protein level of FTH1 was decreased in Ncoa4+/+ hearts compared to both sham-operated Ncoa4+/+ and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts 4 weeks after TAC.
source: The protein level of FTH1 was decreased in Ncoa4+/+ hearts compared to both sham-operated Ncoa4+/+ and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mRNA level of FTH1 was decreased in Ncoa4+/+ hearts 4 weeks after TAC.
source: However, the mRNA level of FTH1 was also decreased in Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cardiac dysfunction and LV chamber dilation were observed in wild-type Ncoa4+/+ hearts during an earlier time course after pressure overload.
source: Cardiac dysfunction and LV chamber dilation were observed in wild-type Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice showed decreased fractional shortening 3 days after surgery compared to the corresponding sham-operated group.
source: Both TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice showed decreased fractional shortening 3 days after surgery compared to the corresponding sham-operated group.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in fractional shortening between TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice 3 days after TAC.
source: However, there was no significant difference in fractional shortening between TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, suggesting mild cardiac dysfunction observed in both groups 3 days after TAC was due to acute response to pressure overload.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The protein level of FTH1 decreased from postoperative day 5 compared to sham-operated hearts.
source: The protein level of FTH1 decreased from postoperative day 5 compared to sham-operated hearts, while the level of Fth1 mRNA increased 5 and 7 days after TAC and decreased 4 weeks after TAC (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The level of Fth1 mRNA increased 5 and 7 days after TAC and decreased 4 weeks after TAC.
source: The protein level of FTH1 decreased from postoperative day 5 compared to sham-operated hearts, while the level of Fth1 mRNA increased 5 and 7 days after TAC and decreased 4 weeks after TAC (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the TAC-operated hearts, the number of LC3B- and FTH1-positive dots increased after postoperative day 5 and then declined 4 weeks after TAC.
source: In the TAC-operated hearts, the number of LC3B (a marker of an autophagosome)- and FTH1-positive dots increased after postoperative day 5 and then declined 4 weeks after TAC (day 7 versus 4 weeks, p<0.0001), and that of LAMP2a (a marker of a lysosome)- and FTH1-positive dots increased 7 days after TAC (Figure 2E,F,G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The number of LAMP2a- and FTH1-positive dots increased 7 days after TAC.
source: In the TAC-operated hearts, the number of LC3B (a marker of an autophagosome)- and FTH1-positive dots increased after postoperative day 5 and then declined 4 weeks after TAC (day 7 versus 4 weeks, p<0.0001), and that of LAMP2a (a marker of a lysosome)- and FTH1-positive dots increased 7 days after TAC (Figure 2E,F,G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The ablation of Ncoa4 attenuated the downregulation of FTH1 protein in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts 7 days after TAC.
source: The ablation of Ncoa4 attenuated the downregulation of FTH1 protein and upregulation of Fth1 mRNA in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ablation of Ncoa4 attenuated the upregulation of Fth1 mRNA in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts 7 days after TAC.
source: The ablation of Ncoa4 attenuated the downregulation of FTH1 protein and upregulation of Fth1 mRNA in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The number of LC3B- and FTH1-positive dots decreased in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts compared to Ncoa4+/+ hearts 7 days after TAC.
source: The number of LC3B- and FTH1-positive dots and the number of LAMP2a- and FTH1-positive dots decreased in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts compared to Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 3C,D,E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The number of LAMP2a- and FTH1-positive dots decreased in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts compared to Ncoa4+/+ hearts 7 days after TAC.
source: The number of LC3B- and FTH1-positive dots and the number of LAMP2a- and FTH1-positive dots decreased in TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts compared to Ncoa4+/+ hearts (Figure 3C,D,E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: There were no significant differences in hematological parameters between any groups of cardiomyocyte-specific NCOA4-deficient mice.
source: There were no significant differences in hematological parameters, serum iron, and transferrin saturation between any groups.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: Pressure overload reduced serum ferritin compared to the corresponding sham-operated group.
source: Pressure overload reduced serum ferritin compared to the corresponding sham-operated group, but there was no significant difference between TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in serum ferritin between TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice.
source: Pressure overload reduced serum ferritin compared to the corresponding sham-operated group, but there was no significant difference between TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: TAC decreased the level of total non-heme iron in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– livers.
source: TAC decreased the level of total non-heme iron in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– livers, but there was no significant difference in the level between Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TAC increased the serum IL-6 level in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, which was higher in Ncoa4+/+ than that in Ncoa4–/–.
source: TAC increased the serum IL-6 level in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– mice, which was higher in Ncoa4+/+ than that in Ncoa4–/– (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pressure overload decreased the total non-heme iron content in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– hearts.
source: Pressure overload decreased the total non-heme iron content in both Ncoa4+/+ and Ncoa4–/– hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of ferrous iron in Ncoa4+/+ hearts was higher than that in Ncoa4–/– hearts under pressure overload.
source: The level of ferrous iron in Ncoa4+/+ hearts was higher than that in Ncoa4–/– hearts under pressure overload, whereas the level of ferric iron was lower in Ncoa4+/+ hearts than in Ncoa4–/– hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of ferric iron was lower in Ncoa4+/+ hearts than in Ncoa4–/– hearts under pressure overload.
source: The level of ferrous iron in Ncoa4+/+ hearts was higher than that in Ncoa4–/– hearts under pressure overload, whereas the level of ferric iron was lower in Ncoa4+/+ hearts than in Ncoa4–/– hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ratio of ferrous iron to FTH1 was higher in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts than in the sham-operated controls and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts.
source: The ratio of ferrous iron to FTH1, which represents the non-binding fraction of ferrous iron to FTH1, was higher in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts than in the sham-operated controls and TAC-operated Ncoa4–/– hearts, suggesting free ferrous iron overload in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The levels of proteins related to intracellular iron metabolism such as IREB2, SLC40A1, and TFRC showed no differences between TAC-operated groups.
source: The levels of proteins related to intracellular iron metabolism such as IREB2, SLC40A1, and TFRC showed no differences between TAC-operated groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were no significant differences in the mRNA levels of Tfrc, Slc11a2, Cdc14a, and Cdc42bpa between TAC-operated groups.
source: There were no significant differences in the mRNA levels of Tfrc, Slc11a2, Cdc14a, and Cdc42bpa between TAC-operated groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The binding of IRP with the 5' UTR of Slc40a1 exhibited no difference between TAC-operated groups.
source: The binding of IRP with the 5' UTR of Slc40a1 exhibited no difference between TAC-operated groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: IRP system is impaired in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice.
source: These suggest that IRP system is impaired in TAC-operated Ncoa4+/+ mice.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing no differences in IRP-related proteins and mRNA despite changes in iron levels.

claim: In Ncoa4+/+ hearts, pressure overload increased the levels of malondialdehyde (MDA).
source: In Ncoa4+/+ hearts, pressure overload increased the levels of malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE)-positive area; markers for lipid peroxidation (Ayala et al., 2014; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Ncoa4+/+ hearts, pressure overload increased 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE)-positive area.
source: In Ncoa4+/+ hearts, pressure overload increased the levels of malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE)-positive area; markers for lipid peroxidation (Ayala et al., 2014; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: MDA and 4-HNE markers were attenuated in Ncoa4–/– hearts after pressure overload.
source: In contrast, these markers were attenuated in Ncoa4–/– hearts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.
